newsitem.title: GERMANY: Window-dressing at odds with EMU test--Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: Window-dressing at odds with EMU test--Tietmeyer.

text.p: - Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on Monday took a stand against possible attempts by European Union countries to "window-dress" their economic data to be sure of make the grade to launch the Euro in January 1999.

"The (EMI) European Monetary Institute should not and will not let itself be blinded by one year's results. This is not a question of window-dressing, but rather of solidity. It is a question of durability and sustainability," he said.
His comments were made in a speech delivered to a political forum in Bonn, which was made available in advance.

At the same time, Tietmeyer defended the need for precise limits on economic performance in order to qualify for currency union. He said the criteria to determine which states could enter monetary union were rather too generous than too strict.
"Numerical limits are important so that the convergence criteria can fulfil their selective function and give no leeway for randomness or political give and take," Tietmeyer said.
"Viewed as a unit, they test the starting point and maturity of a country in terms of stability. And in this all criteria are important," he said.
But he added that this did not mean that the numbers were sacrosanct and could be viewed in isolation: "This should of course not mean falling into a naive faith in numbers."
The Maastricht Treaty sets down various requirements on currency, economic and fiscal developments which would-be EMU entrants must fulfil by the end of 1997 in order to take part in the Euro launch.

Viewed as the toughest are the criteria which demand that a country's debt level is not more than 60 percent of gross domestic product and that the national budget deficit does not exceed three percent of GDP.

Tietmeyer said it was essential for the success of the European Economic and Monetary Union that all countries taking part in the single currency from the start showed the same commitment to fiscal discipline.
"That is why the choice of participants who fit together is such a central point. Success or failure hinges on this to a decisive extent," he said.
